historical_timeline.summary: Nurse radiographer with mobile X-ray units in the First World War.
Doctorate on the alpha rays of polonium; married Frédéric Joliot the next year.
Death of her mother from aplastic anemia attributed to radiation.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Frédéric Joliot.
Undersecretary of State for Scientific Research; professor from 1937.
Recovering from tuberculosis in Switzerland during the war.
Director of the Radium Institute; a polonium capsule exploded on her bench.
Visible decline in her health from shortly after this year.
Died of leukemia in Paris; her leukemia is attributed to occupational radiation.

claims.statement: Irène Curie was born in Paris on 12 September 1897, the elder daughter of the physicist Pierre Curie and his wife, a physicist who also worked with radioactive materials.
During the First World War she served as a nurse radiographer, operating X-ray machines in mobile field hospitals alongside her mother.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Start of her occupational exposure to ionizing radiation; anchors the modern occupational history.

claims.statement: She became a Doctor of Science in 1925 with a thesis on the alpha rays of polonium, and in 1926 married Frédéric Joliot; the couple joined their surnames and worked together on natural and artificial radioactivity and nuclear physics.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors decades of laboratory work with polonium and other radioactive sources.

claims.statement: In 1935 she and Frédéric Joliot shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their synthesis of new radioactive elements, after showing that bombarding aluminum foil with alpha particles produced artificial radioactivity.

In 1936 she was appointed Undersecretary of State for Scientific Research; she became a professor in the Faculty of Science in Paris in 1937, and her research on the action of neutrons on heavy elements in 1938 was an important step toward the discovery of nuclear fission.
She and Frédéric Joliot had a daughter and a son.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented history only; the children are not named and play no part in the modern episode.

claims.statement: She had always been of unstable health, and the couple took regular trips to the countryside to help her condition.
During the Second World War she spent time in Switzerland recovering from tuberculosis, and in 1944 brought her children with her to Switzerland.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern history of treated pulmonary tuberculosis and the reduced lung gas transfer found on testing.

claims.statement: In 1946 she became director of the Radium Institute; as a commissioner for atomic energy for six years she took part in building the first French atomic pile in 1948, and she drew up the plans for the large nuclear physics center at Orsay.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern work history as a laboratory director.

claims.statement: In 1946 a capsule of polonium exploded on her laboratory bench.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern history of a sealed-source accident in her laboratory; no dose estimate from the incident is documented.

claims.statement: Smithsonian magazine reported that the 1946 polonium accident is thought to have possibly been responsible for her death from leukemia ten years later, and that she may have been the first person to die of polonium poisoning.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; the modern episode records the accident as part of an occupational history and does not attribute the leukemia to one event.

claims.statement: Her leukemia is usually attributed to over-exposure to X-rays during the First World War and to radioactive materials during her life of research.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation, widely repeated; why the modern episode takes an occupational radiation history and treats the leukemia as exposure-related.

claims.statement: Shortly after 1950 her health declined visibly.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the timing of the index visit and the synthetic presenting illness.

claims.statement: A stay in the mountains in 1956 brought no improvement, and she died of leukemia shortly after.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history. No modern visit is placed in 1956 in the true frame.

claims.statement: She died of leukemia in Paris on 17 March 1956, at the age of 58.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; the type of leukemia is not stated in the cited sources, and the modern subtype is synthetic.

claims.statement: Her mother died on 4 July 1934; the director of the sanatorium where she died reported an aplastic pernicious anemia of rapid, feverish development, in which the bone marrow did not react, probably because it had been injured by a long accumulation of radiations.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history: bone marrow failure attributed to radiation in a parent who worked with radioactive materials.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize acute myeloid leukemia in a 58-year-old physicist whose tiredness, bruising and bleeding gums come with pancytopenia and blasts on the smear, and care for it on the NCCN AML guideline and the ELN 1951 recommendations: same-week hematology review with coagulation tests to exclude acute promyelocytic leukemia; bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular testing; classification by both the WHO 1951 and ICC 1951 systems and ELN 1951 genetic risk, deciding how to describe leukemia after occupational rather than therapeutic radiation; a fitness assessment (performance status, comorbidity, lung function after old tuberculosis); azacitidine with venetoclax for a patient unfit for intensive induction, with the dose reduced for posaconazole and tumor lysis precautions; transfusion support with irradiated products; antifungal, antiviral and antibacterial prophylaxis and a febrile neutropenia plan; response assessment at the day-22 marrow and count recovery; early evaluation for allogeneic stem cell transplant; specialist palliative care from the start; and an occupational health history that asks for her dose records, records the employer's duty to keep and release them, and documents a laboratory accident with a polonium source.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient visit for two months of tiredness, bruising and bleeding gums: blood count with blasts on the smear, and urgent hematology referral
Hematology consultation and bone marrow biopsy: diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia, transfusion, and pre-treatment work-up

Same-day sick visit for nausea, vomiting and constipation during cycle 1
Day 22 of cycle 1: bone marrow response, transfusion and infection review, and stopping venetoclax for count recovery
Periodic adult preventive visit during AML therapy

assessment_plan.display: Acute myeloid leukemia with mutated TP53 and a complex karyotype; ELN 1951 adverse risk
assessment_plan.assessment: Cytogenetics show a complex karyotype with loss of chromosome 5q material and of chromosome 7 (45,XX,del(5)(q14q34),-7,-17,+mar in 16 of 20 cells), and the molecular panel shows a TP53 mutation at a variant allele frequency of 41 percent, with no NPM1, FLT3, IDH1, IDH2 or CEBPA mutation. By the WHO 1951 classification this is AML, myelodysplasia-related (defined by the complex karyotype); by the ICC 1951 it is AML with mutated TP53. Neither system's post-cytotoxic-therapy (therapy-related) label applies, because that label requires earlier chemotherapy or radiotherapy given as treatment, whereas her exposure was occupational; we record the leukemia as following occupational exposure to ionizing radiation, and its genetics are those typical of radiation-associated and therapy-related myeloid neoplasms. ELN 1951 genetic risk is adverse. Fitness: ECOG 2 and a DLCO of 58 percent of predicted (HCT-CI score 3) make her ineligible for intensive induction under the VIALE-A criteria; intensive chemotherapy also gives poor results in TP53-mutated AML. After discussing the options, including intensive induction and clinical trials (none open to her here), she chooses azacitidine with venetoclax, aiming for remission and an allogeneic transplant. Dr. Engquist-Mensah's team will lead treatment

For three days she has felt queasy for most of the day, and she vomited twice yesterday, about an hour after her evening meal; the venetoclax tablets had been taken with breakfast and stayed down. She has had no chills, cough, sore throat, mouth sores, painful urination, diarrhea, or rectal pain. Her gums ooze a little when she brushes, and she has new small bruises on her shins. She is drinking about a liter and a half a day. She takes posaconazole, acyclovir, levofloxacin and allopurinol as prescribed.

referral.question: Pancytopenia with 12 percent blasts on the blood smear in a 58-year-old nuclear physicist with about four decades of occupational exposure to ionizing radiation and treated tuberculosis. Please confirm the diagnosis by bone marrow, classify it, assess her fitness, and plan treatment, transfusion and infection prevention
referral.urgency: Urgent, within two days; she is stable and afebrile today and has a written fever and bleeding plan
referral.pertinent_history: Two months of increasing tiredness, easy bruising, bleeding gums when brushing, and two chest colds that were slow to clear; no fever now. She is director of a university radioactivity laboratory; she operated X-ray equipment early in her career, has worked with polonium and other sealed and unsealed sources for decades, and about ten years ago a sealed polonium source ruptured on her bench. She wears a dosimetry badge and is asking for her records. Pulmonary tuberculosis in her forties, treated to completion. Her mother, a physicist who also worked with radioactive materials, died of aplastic anemia attributed to radiation. No medicines; no known allergy. Today: weight 54.0 kg, blood pressure 118/70, pulse 96, temperature 37.2 °C; pale, with bruises on the shins and gum petechiae; no lymph nodes or enlarged spleen. Results today: white cells 2.1 with neutrophils 0.6 x10^3/uL, hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL with MCV 104 fL, platelets 38 x10^3/uL, blasts 12 percent on the smear; sodium 139, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 0.78 mg/dL, eGFR 88, calcium 9.2 mg/dL, ALT 22 U/L, bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, LDH 412 U/L, uric acid 6.4 mg/dL. consultant_note.history: Mrs. Joliot-Curie, a 58-year-old nuclear physicist, is seen at the request of Dr. Marchand-Ellis two days after pancytopenia with circulating blasts was found. She describes two months of tiredness, then bruising and gum bleeding, and in the last two days breathlessness on one flight of stairs. She has had no fever, bone pain, or weight loss. Her occupational history is long: X-ray work early in her career, decades of laboratory work with polonium and other radioactive sources, and the rupture of a sealed polonium source on her bench about ten years ago, she does not know what dose she received from it; her monitored doses are recorded by her employer. Pulmonary tuberculosis in her forties was treated to completion, and she has been breathless on stairs since. She has never smoked and takes no medicines. Her mother died of aplastic anemia attributed to radiation. She wants the evidence and the numbers, and wants to keep working with her mind for as long as she can
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Marchand-Ellis's intake note and results. Today: white cells 1.9 with neutrophils 0.5 x10^3/uL, hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL, platelets 22 x10^3/uL, blasts 14 percent on the smear; INR 1.1, fibrinogen 310 mg/dL. Bone marrow aspirate this morning: 34 percent myeloblasts with dysplasia in the red cell and megakaryocyte lines; flow cytometry shows myeloid blasts positive for CD34, CD117, CD13, CD33, HLA-DR and MPO; rapid PML::RARA FISH negative. Cytogenetics and a myeloid next-generation sequencing panel are pending. Chest X-ray this morning: old fibrotic scarring at the right apex, no active disease

assessment.assessment: Confirmed: 34 percent marrow myeloblasts of myeloid phenotype. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is excluded by the phenotype, the normal coagulation tests and the negative rapid PML::RARA test, so there is no need for emergency all-trans retinoic acid. The multilineage dysplasia and the macrocytosis suggest a leukemia arising from a damaged marrow. Classification and risk await the cytogenetics and molecular panel. After long exposure to ionizing radiation, the most likely findings are a complex karyotype, loss of 5q or 7, and a TP53 mutation, which would mean adverse risk. The WHO and ICC labels for leukemia after cytotoxic therapy (therapy-related) are defined by earlier chemotherapy or radiotherapy given as treatment, so her leukemia should be classified by its genetics and her occupational exposure recorded in the history rather than as a therapy-related label

ECOG 1 today, but her lung reserve may be reduced by old tuberculous scarring; lung function with diffusing capacity, an echocardiogram and an ECG are needed before choosing induction. If her diffusing capacity is 65 percent of predicted or less, or her performance status falls to 2, she would be outside the trial definition of fitness for intensive induction. The chest X-ray shows no active tuberculosis; treated disease needs no preventive therapy, but new respiratory symptoms during neutropenia should be investigated promptly
A recognized risk factor for myeloid leukemia, consistent with her history. Her employer must keep her dose records and give them to her on request

recommendations: Cytogenetics, a myeloid sequencing panel (including FLT3, NPM1, IDH1, IDH2, TP53 and CEBPA) and FISH from today's marrow; classify by both WHO 1951 and ICC 1951 and assign ELN 1951 genetic risk when results are back, in about ten days
Echocardiogram, ECG and lung function tests with diffusing capacity on the day of the results review

If the genetics are adverse (for example TP53-mutated or complex karyotype) or she is unfit for intensive induction, azacitidine 75 mg/m2 on days 1 to 7 with venetoclax in 28-day cycles; if she is fit and the genetics are favorable or intermediate, intensive induction would be offered. Either way, discuss clinical trials

With venetoclax, admit for the ramp-up with tumor lysis monitoring, allopurinol and fluids; with posaconazole, give venetoclax 70 mg daily after the ramp-up; marrow on day 21 to 28, holding venetoclax until counts recover if the marrow is clear

Transfusion: irradiated, leukoreduced products; red cells one unit at a time for hemoglobin below 7 to 8 g/dL or symptoms (one unit today); platelets for a count below 10 x10^3/uL or bleeding; no platelet transfusion was needed for today's biopsy
Prophylaxis once treatment starts: posaconazole (mold-active, because neutropenia will be prolonged), acyclovir, and levofloxacin while neutrophils are below 0.5; a written fever plan now
Hepatitis B (surface antigen, core antibody, surface antibody), hepatitis C and HIV tests before therapy, and HLA typing now

She is a potential candidate for a reduced-intensity allogeneic transplant in first remission, especially with adverse genetics: transplant center evaluation and an unrelated donor search at the start of treatment
